title: My Wife is An Actress
full_review:
The frothy romantic comedy "My Wife Is An Actress" (Sony Pictures Classics) throws an average husband into a jealous tizzy when his popular movie star wife plays opposite a suave, international artiste in her next film.

Written, directed and starring Yvan Attal, the French film pits the glamour of movie making against the real world, with Attal's character, also named Yvan, stuck in the middle. Madly in love with his wife Charlotte (played by real-life wife Charlotte Gainsbourg), sports writer Yvan is becoming increasingly jealous of his wife's professional life.

First it is the inconvenience of fans expecting autographs and photos at any time. When the couple is pulled over by a policeman, the cop is mesmerized by Charlotte and, of course, no ticket is issued. Then it is her celebrity status, which gets her into a previously booked posh restaurant without any trouble. These are minor annoyances, certainly, with some advantages.

But his vexation turns into frustration when he sees Charlotte in a racy scene from her last movie. Now Charlotte will be filming in London with the well-known and handsome John (Terence Stamp), an actor who makes all the women swoon. At first, Yvan is able to keep his composure, but then the green-headed monster rears its ugly face and Yvan stoops to concocting silly schemes to test his wife's fidelity.

The film is interesting in its humorous, but on some levels profound, examination of the fine line between passion and pretence. Tabloid news exposes all kinds of affairs that began during filmmaking, so Yvan's suspicions are not completely out of the question. What Attal does in the script is to couch this notion of sexual jealousy in a screwball comedy that exaggerates the situation but still has plenty of heart. However, once the setup is complete, the narrative's flaws begin to show. By the time they start to consider extramarital opportunities, inflaming jealousies and suspicion, the film sags. The nagging question of "where is this going?" creeps into the viewer's mind and the anti-climactic ending fizzles when it should have popped.

Nonetheless, there are still some good things to enjoy. Attal is charming in his neurosis (which bares some comparison to Woody Allen) -- and ruggedly handsome good looks (which does not). Casting his real-life wife as his on-screen wife has a certain interesting quality that gives the film an edge and makes for a relaxed give-and-take between the characters. But Gainsbourg is flat, making it difficult to believe that she really is a sought-after super-celebrity. Stamp makes the most of his one-dimensional role, presenting the shallow John as a man who takes himself � and his limited talent �- way too seriously. It is fun to watch him preen and attempt to seduce Charlotte in the most obvious ways.

A subplot involving Yvan's pregnant sister Nathalie (Noemie Lvovsky) and her husband Vincent (Laurent Bateau) provides some humor regarding Judaism and circumcision. This more "normal" couple acts as a foil for the first, contrasting the average fights between husband and wife to Yvan and Charlotte's problems of movie-star jealousies.

Attal finds humor in other situations as well such as dance club bouncers, nosy strangers and superficial acting classes. But the material is stretched thin and becomes a bit monotonous. And while a particular nude scene may draw guffaws from some viewers, others may be a bit startled by its brashness.

Subtitles.

Due to brief sexual encounters, full frontal nudity and sporadic rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

Navarro is on the staff of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Office for Film and Broadcasting.
